title: Learning with Expert Advice
journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
abstract: Surveys of inflation forecasts show that expectations combine forward-looking and backward-looking elements. This contradicts conventional wisdom: in the presence of rational agents, adaptive agents would be driven out of the market. In our paper, we rationalize this finding in an equilibrium framework. Our model has two types of agents, one having rational expectations and the other using adaptive learning. The proportion of these agents in the population evolves according to their past forecasting performance. We show that even an underparameterized learning algorithm survives competition with rational expectations.
summary_en: Survey-based forecasts of inflation typically blend forward-looking and backward-looking elements, contradicting the textbook prediction that rational agents should drive adaptive forecasters out of the market. Molnár builds a model with both agent types whose population shares evolve based on past forecasting accuracy. She shows that even a deliberately under-parameterised adaptive-learning rule can survive in equilibrium against rational expectations — providing a microfounded reason why real-world inflation expectations stay heterogeneous, and why central-bank surveys consistently find a mix of expectation types.
data_used: Theoretical model. Calibration draws on stylised features of inflation-expectation surveys (Survey of Professional Forecasters, Michigan Survey) showing the persistent coexistence of forward- and backward-looking forecasters.
policy_relevance: MNB's inflation-expectations surveys consistently show heterogeneous forecasters. The paper provides a theoretical justification for treating this mix as a stable equilibrium feature, not a transitional artefact — which matters when the central bank communicates forecasts and decides how much weight to give backward-looking versus forward-looking signals in policy decisions.
